title: Merge Operations for Minimum Travel Time
summary: Given a straight road of length l km, with n signs at positions in strictly increasing order, and travel times between consecutive signs, you must perform exactly k merge operations.
statement: Given a straight road of length l km, with n signs at positions in strictly increasing order, and travel times between consecutive signs, you must perform exactly k merge operations. Each merge operation involves selecting any two adjacent signs at indices i and i + 1 (where i > 0 and i + 1 < n ), updating the travel time at the sign at index i + 1 to be the sum of the travel times at indices i and i + 1 , and then removing the sign at index i . The task is to determine the minimum total travel time required to travel from the start (position 0) to the end (position l ) of the road after performing exactly k merges.
constraints: Positions are strictly increasing from 0 to l; n <= 50 and exactly k <= 10 internal signs must be removed.
Removing sign i adds its per-km time to the next sign’s time; endpoints cannot be removed.
After exactly k merges, minimize sum(distance segment * current per-km time).
hints: A retained sign’s rate equals the sum of original rates since the preceding retained sign, so pricing its outgoing segment needs the previous two retained boundaries.
Use prefix sums and DP states (previous retained, last retained, removed count), extending to each later retained sign.
Charge distance(last,current) times the accumulated rate at last, add skipped signs to the merge count, and require the endpoint with exactly k removals.
Every final retained-sign sequence uniquely defines all merged rate groups, and every legal merge result corresponds to one such sequence.
editorial: Every final retained-sign sequence uniquely defines all merged rate groups, and every legal merge result corresponds to one such sequence.

tests.explanation: Removing position three makes rates [5,11] on distances eight and two, totaling 62.
Removing position one yields segment costs 16, 12, and 6, totaling 34.
